title: The epistemic debt of generative AI - Nature Machine Intelligence
gist: A short comment coins 'epistemic debt' -- the compounding gap between what generative-AI-assisted authors present and what they can actually defend or understand -- as a systemic risk that widens as more work is built on unverified AI output.

insights.claim: When people use generative AI for cognitive tasks without investing the time to understand its output, a gap opens between what they present as their own work and what they can actually defend or justify -- and this gap is framed as a distinct, nameable form of debt.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Names a trackable risk category for enterprises deploying generative AI in knowledge work, and gives a framework for AI-adoption governance plus a potential opening for AI-verification and provenance-tooling vendors.
insights.quote: When authors use generative AI in cognitive tasks, without spending time and effort to understand the output, a gap opens between what they present and what they can defend.

insights.claim: Epistemic debt compounds because subsequent work gets built on top of unverified AI-generated output, so unexamined errors or unjustified claims propagate and the gap between what is presented and what is actually defensible keeps widening over time.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Implies the cost of un-vetted generative-AI use is back-loaded and cumulative rather than immediate, similar to technical debt -- a risk multiplier for firms with high GenAI usage in long content or knowledge pipelines (research, journalism, financial analysis, legal work).
insights.quote: This gap widens as further work is built on top, resulting in epistemic debt.

insights.claim: The 'epistemic debt' framing implicitly borrows the economics of technical debt in software engineering, suggesting that unverified generative-AI output, like unrefactored code, eventually requires a costly 'repayment' step -- verification, correction or re-derivation -- before further work can be trusted.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: If this framing catches on, it could become a standard vocabulary term investors and auditors use to describe and price AI-adoption risk inside organizations, similar to how 'technical debt' became a due-diligence concept for software assets.
